records.title: The Butterfly Lovers (Liang Shanbo and Zhu Yingtai)
records.summary: One of the Four Great Folktales of China, young maiden Zhu Yingtai disguises herself as a male scholar to attend the academy in Hangzhou during the Eastern Jin dynasty. There, she forms a profound bond with fellow scholar Liang Shanbo, who remains oblivious to her true gender for three years of study. When Liang finally discovers her identity and seeks her hand in marriage, Zhu's family has already betrothed her to a wealthy nobleman. Dying of a broken heart, Liang is buried beside the road. On her wedding day, a storm forces Zhu's procession past his tomb; the earth opens, and Zhu leaps into the grave. From the mound, a pair of radiant butterflies emerge, fluttering into the sky together in eternal harmony.
records.historical_period: Eastern Jin Dynasty setting (c. 4th Century CE, popularized in Tang and Song ballads)

records.title: Chang'e Flies to the Moon (Mid-Autumn Festival)
records.summary: Following his heroic deed of shooting down nine scorching suns with his divine bow, the master archer Hou Yi received an elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West (Xi Wangmu). Not wishing to ascend to the heavens without his beloved wife Chang'e, Hou Yi entrusted the vial to her for safekeeping. When Hou Yi's envious apprentice Feng Meng broke into their pavilion with a sword demanding the potion, Chang'e drank the elixir to prevent it from falling into evil hands. Instantly becoming weightless, she floated into the night sky, settling on the Moon to be near the mortal earth. Accompanied by the Jade Rabbit who pounds herbs of life beneath the cinnamon tree, she is commemorated during the Mid-Autumn Festival with mooncakes.
alternate_names: The Moon Goddess and the Jade Rabbit
records.historical_period: Warring States / Han Dynasty (recorded in Huainanzi c. 139 BCE)
records.region_or_community: Central Plains of China, nationwide Chinese cultural festival

records.title: The Legend of the White Snake (Madam White Snake)
records.summary: After a thousand years of Taoist cultivation on Mount Emei, a thousand-year-old white serpent spirit named Bai Suzhen transforms into a radiant woman and falls in love with gentle apothecary scholar Xu Xian beneath a silk umbrella during a rainstorm at the Broken Bridge on West Lake. Living as devoted spouses in Zhenjiang, Bai Suzhen uses her magical medical herbs to cure plague victims. However, the dogmatic Buddhist abbot Fahai of Jinshan Temple intervenes, exposing her true serpent form with realgar wine and imprisoning her beneath the Leifeng Pagoda on West Lake, until her loyal green snake sister Xiaoqing breaks the pagoda stones to free her.
records.historical_period: Song Dynasty oral tradition (compiled in Feng Menglong's Jingshi Tongyan, 1624)
records.region_or_community: Hangzhou and Zhenjiang, Zhejiang and Jiangsu Provinces

records.title: The Cowherd and the Weaver Girl (Niulang and Zhinü)
records.summary: Celebrated during the Qixi Festival (Double Seventh), Niulang is an honest, orphaned cowherd guided by his loyal speaking ox to a heavenly lake, where seven celestial weaver maidens are bathing. Niulang meets Zhinü, the seventh daughter of the Heavenly Queen who weaves clouds and tapestries across the sky; the two marry in mortal bliss and raise twin children. Enraged that a celestial maiden has wed a mortal, the Queen Mother of the West drags Zhinü back to the heavens. Pursuing her through the skies on cowhide sandals, Niulang is separated from his wife when the Queen scratches a silver river—the Milky Way—across the cosmos, allowing them to reunite only once a year on the seventh day of the seventh lunar month across a bridge formed by sympathetic magpies.
alternate_names: The Weaver Maiden and the Herdsman
records.historical_period: Zhou / Han Dynasty (recorded in the Classic of Poetry, Shijing c. 6th Century BCE)
records.region_or_community: Shandong, Henan, and Yellow River heartland

records.title: Hou Yi Shoots the Nine Suns
records.summary: In primordial antiquity, the ten sons of the sun goddess Xihe dwelt in the branches of the colossal Fusang tree in the eastern sea, each scheduled to cross the sky in sequence. One fateful day, bored with their routine, all ten suns rose simultaneously into the heavens, scorching the earth, boiling river waters, withering crops, and unleashing ferocious fire demons upon humanity. Emperor Yao summoned the divine archer Hou Yi, gifted with a vermilion bow and white feathered arrows. Climbing Mount Kunlun, Hou Yi shot down nine suns one by one, their bodies falling as giant golden three-legged crows, leaving a solitary sun in the sky so the earth would have warmth without destruction.
alternate_names: The Ten Suns of the Fusang Tree
records.historical_period: Pre-Qin to Han Dynasty (Classic of Mountains and Seas, Shanhaijing)
records.region_or_community: Ancient Central Plains and Mount Kunlun mythological region

records.title: Nezha Conquers the Dragon King of the Eastern Sea
records.summary: Born as a miraculous ball of flesh to General Li Jing after three years of gestation, Nezha is an avatar of the divine Lingzhu, wielding the Universe Ring (Qiankun Quan) and Red Armillary Sash (Huntian Ling) gifted by Taoist immortal Taiyi Zhenren. While washing his sash in the Nine Bends River, the vibrations rock the crystal palace of the Dragon King Ao Guang. When the Dragon Prince Ao Bing attacks him with vicious sea monsters, Nezha defeats the prince and extracts his dragon spine. To protect his father and city from the Dragon King's drowning tidal deluges, Nezha selflessly cuts off his own flesh and carves out his bones to return to his parents, before being resurrected by his master from lotus roots.
records.historical_period: Ming Dynasty (compiled c. 16th Century in Investiture of the Gods, Fengshen Yanyi)

records.title: Sun Wukong and the Peaches of Immortality
records.summary: Born from a divine stone atop the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, Sun Wukong, the Monkey King, masters Taoist seventy-two transformations, somersault clouds, and wields the compliant golden-hooped iron staff (Ruyi Jingu Bang) dredged from the Eastern Sea. Granted the celestial office of Keeper of the Heavenly Peach Garden by the Jade Emperor, Wukong discovers the Queen Mother's banquet excludes him. In rebellion, he feasts on the three-thousand-year celestial peaches, guzzles Laozi's golden immortality pills, and trashes the celestial palace. Unharmed by lightning or heavenly blades, Wukong is trapped only when the Buddha wagers the monkey cannot leap from his palm, pinning him beneath Five Elements Mountain.
alternate_names: The Monkey King of Journey to the West

records.title: Meng Jiang Nü Weeps at the Great Wall
records.summary: During the brutal reign of Qin Shi Huang, young scholar Fan Qiliang was forcibly conscripted on his wedding day to build the Great Wall of China in the freezing northern wilderness. When winter arrived, his devoted bride Meng Jiang Nü wove warm padded winter clothes and walked thousands of li on foot through blizzards to deliver them. Arriving at the mountain pass of Shanhaiguan, she discovered her husband had already died of exhaustion and was buried inside the wall's ramparts. Devastated, she collapsed against the stone and wept for three days and nights; her sorrow shook the earth, causing four hundred miles of the Great Wall to collapse, exposing the bones of her husband.
alternate_names: The Tears that Crumbled the Great Wall
records.historical_period: Qin Dynasty setting (c. 221 BCE, compiled in Tang and Song ballads)

records.title: The Nian Monster and the Spring Festival
records.summary: In ancient times, a ferocious beast named Nian with sharp horns and a lion-like muzzle dwelt at the bottom of the sea, ascending to land on New Year's Eve to devour livestock and villagers in coastal towns. One winter evening, a wandering grey-haired beggar informed an old woman that the beast harbored three secret terrors: the color red, bright firelight, and loud concussive noises. When the monster approached the village, it was confronted by crimson banners affixed to doors, blazing torches, and explosive bamboo fires popping fiercely. Terrified, the monster fled into the ocean depths, establishing the enduring Chinese New Year customs of red couplets, firecrackers, and dragon dances (Guo Nian).
alternate_names: How Chinese New Year Was Born (Guo Nian)
records.historical_period: Ancient Folk Tradition (recorded in Qing Dynasty folk primers)

records.title: Pan Gu Separates Heaven and Earth
records.summary: In the beginning before time existed, the cosmos was a boundless, swirling black egg containing chaos (Hundun), inside which the giant Pan Gu slept and grew for eighteen thousand years. Awakening in darkness, Pan Gu seized a colossal divine axe and cleaved the eggshell apart: the clear, light Yang energy rose upward to become the azure Heavens, while the murky, heavy Yin energy sank down to form the solid Earth. Fearing they would merge together again, Pan Gu stood between them, holding up the sky and growing ten feet taller every day for eighteen thousand more years. When the cosmos was stabilized, Pan Gu died of exhaustion; his breath became the wind and clouds, his left eye the sun, his right eye the moon, his blood the flowing rivers, his muscles the fertile soils, and his fleas the human race.
records.historical_period: Three Kingdoms Period (recorded by Xu Zheng in Sanwu Liji c. 3rd Century CE)
records.region_or_community: Southern China and Central Plains, nationwide Chinese cosmology
